e.etymology: An American boys' name of the 1970s that ends in -shon, a spelling of Shawn, like Deshawn and Rashon. Vashon is also a surname and an island in Washington's Puget Sound.
An English surname from Middle English modi, bold or proud, first a nickname. Its use as a first name in the late 1800s coincided with the fame of the evangelist Dwight L. Moody.
e.note: Identical to the everyday adjective moody, so jokes about mood swings come easily.

assoc.t: moody, the word for given to bad moods

e.etymology: A variant of Malvina, which the Scottish poet James Macpherson coined in his Ossian poems of the 1760s from Gaelic mala-mhin, smooth brow. It has also served as a feminine form of Melvin.
A phonetic spelling of Chante, an American girls' name modeled on French chante (sung) and on Chantal. It was most used in the 1980s.
In the US a 1970s African-American coinage built from the Sha- opening and the -ika ending, a sister to Shaniqua. A separate Shanika is a Sinhala name used in Sri Lanka.
A phonetic spelling of Chantal, the French name that honors Saint Jeanne de Chantal. Her title came from a place name built on an old Occitan word for stone.
A transposed spelling of Michael, from Hebrew Mikha'el, a rhetorical question meaning who is like God?. Michael is the archangel who leads the heavenly armies.
From Sanskrit candra, moon, also the name of the Hindu moon god. In India it is mostly a man's name or a name element; in the US it became a girls' name in the 1970s.
namesakes: Chandra Wilson (actress, Dr. Bailey on Grey's Anatomy)

e.etymology: An English and Scottish surname from places named in Old English with mor (moor, marsh) and tun (settlement). In 20th-century America it was also a common English stand-in for Moses and Mordecai.
namesakes: Morton Downey Jr. (combative 1980s talk show host)

assoc.t: Morton Salt, the umbrella-girl table salt

e.meaning: of the Lucretius family, from Latin lucrum, gain
e.etymology: The feminine of the Roman family name Lucretius, tied to Latin lucrum, gain or profit. The Lucretia of Roman legend was the noblewoman whose death led to the overthrow of the kings.
namesakes: Lucretia Mott (abolitionist and women's rights leader)
Lucretia Garfield (First Lady, wife of James Garfield)

e.etymology: A spelling of Timmy, the pet form of Timothy, from Greek Timotheos, which joins time (honor) and theos (god).
An American name of the early 1900s, used mostly in the South, built on the Theo- of Theodore with an ending like that of Otis and Odis.
A Low German and Scandinavian pet form of Margaret, alongside Meta and Mette; Margaret comes from Greek margarites, pearl. Metta is also the Pali word for loving-kindness in Buddhism.
namesakes: Metta Sandiford-Artest (NBA player formerly Ron Artest and Metta World Peace)

e.etymology: Given to girls in the American South in the late 1800s, also spelled Icie. It matches the English word icy; where the name came from is not recorded.
e.note: Identical to the adjective icy, which also means cold or unfriendly.

e.etymology: An American girls' name that rose in the early 1980s, when Teela was the warrior heroine of the He-Man and the Masters of the Universe toys and cartoon.

assoc.t: Teela, warrior heroine of He-Man's Masters of the Universe

e.etymology: An American spelling of Dolores, from the Spanish title of the Virgin Mary, Maria de los Dolores, Mary of the Sorrows.
A spelling of Rhonda, a 20th-century name most likely taken from the Rhondda Valley in Wales, whose river name means noisy. Ronda is also a city in southern Spain.
namesakes: Ronda Rousey (UFC champion and WWE wrestler)

assoc.t: Ronda Rousey, UFC champion and wrestler

e.etymology: A 20th-century spelling of Karen, the Danish short form of Katherine, from Greek Aikaterine. The traditional meaning pure comes from a later link with Greek katharos.
namesakes: Karyn Parsons (actress, Hilary on The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air)
e.note: Sounds the same as Karen, now slang for an entitled, complaining woman.

assoc.t: sounds the same as Karen, slang for an entitled complainer

e.etymology: Used in the US from the late 1800s, read either as a feminine form of Allen or as a spelling of Aline, the medieval short form of Adeline.
A J- spelling of Gerald, from the Germanic elements ger (spear) and wald (rule), a name the Normans brought to England. Jerry is the usual short form.
Common in the US in the late 1800s. It is usually linked to Imma, an old Germanic short form of names in Irm- that also lies behind Emma.
namesakes: Ima Hogg (Texas philanthropist and art collector)
e.note: Sounds like the phrase I'm a, which turns many surnames into a joke, as with the real Ima Hogg.

e.etymology: A variant of Tasha, the short form of Natasha. Natasha is the Russian pet form of Natalia, from Latin natale domini, the birthday of the Lord.
A less common spelling of Douglas, the Scottish clan name taken from a river: Gaelic dubh (black, dark) and glais (stream). The double s is the spelling Frederick Douglass chose.

assoc.t: Frederick Douglass, abolitionist, orator and author

e.etymology: An American elaboration of Lana with the French diminutive ending -ette, most used in the 1960s.
A surname used as a first name. The surname goes back to Loy, the medieval short form of Eloy, the French name of Saint Eligius, from Latin eligere, to choose.
From Latin felix, fortunate or happy. In Italy Felice, said feh-LEE-cheh, is a man's name equal to Felix; American families have used it mostly for girls, as a sister form of Felicia.
An American name of the early 1900s that blends the sound of Darrell with the ending of Harold and Gerald.
The Spanish feminine form of Herminius, an ancient Roman family name of uncertain, possibly Etruscan, origin. It is often also connected with the Germanic name Herman.
A spelling of Trudy, the pet form of Gertrude, from the Germanic elements for spear and strength. Trudy and Trudie have long been given as names in their own right.
A respelling of Cornelius, a great Roman family name usually linked to Latin cornu, horn. In the Book of Acts the centurion Cornelius is the first Gentile convert.
